V01-C-001: For decades, researchers assumed that a placebo could work only if the patient believed it to be a genuine drug. That assumption made the placebo ethically awkward, since using one in ordinary practice seemed to require deceiving the patient. In recent years, however, some trials have asked whether the deception is necessary at all, handing patients pills openly described as inert. If findings of relief among such patients hold up, the ethical objection loses much of its force, because a remedy offered honestly involves no deception.
V01-C-002: In ordinary emergency medicine, the patient in greatest danger is treated first, a rule so natural that it rarely needs defending. Disaster triage deliberately abandons that rule when casualties overwhelm the staff and supplies available. Under such conditions, an hour spent on a patient who will probably die anyway is an hour denied to several who could be saved with modest care. Triage officers therefore sort the injured by how much difference treatment will make, a practice that looks callous only until one counts everyone who is waiting.
V01-C-003: When a nineteenth-century physician urged his colleagues to wash their hands between the autopsy room and the maternity ward, many of them refused. Their resistance is usually told as a story of mere arrogance, but it had a more interesting source. No accepted theory of disease at the time explained how invisible matter on the hands could carry illness from a corpse to a mother. A remedy that worked without a reason struck them as a coincidence rather than a discovery, and only when germ theory supplied the mechanism did handwashing become common sense.
V01-C-004: When a kidney becomes available, one way to choose among the many patients waiting is to give it to whoever has waited longest, a rule that is transparent and hard to manipulate. Yet waiting time ignores how well the organ will function in a particular body, so a strict queue can send a scarce kidney where it will fail within a few years. The opposite rule, allocating each organ to the patient expected to gain the most years from it, corrects this flaw but tends to favour the young and the otherwise healthy. Practical schemes therefore tend to blend the two principles, accepting some loss of efficiency to stay fair and some loss of simple fairness to avoid wasting organs.
V01-C-005: The word quarantine comes from the Italian for forty days, the period that ships arriving from plague-stricken ports were once made to wait before landing. Nobody at the time knew how plague spread, and the figure of forty may have owed more to tradition than to any observation of the disease. Even so, the practice often worked, because a delay long enough for infected passengers to fall ill revealed the danger before it came ashore. Quarantine is thus an early case of a public health measure that succeeded for reasons its inventors could not have stated.
V01-C-006: Walk through almost any public park and you will find bare strips of earth cutting across the lawns where no path was ever laid. Planners call these desire paths, and for a long time they treated them as damage to be fenced off or replanted. Some designers now take the opposite view, reading such tracks as a free survey of where people actually want to go. On this view, a new campus might open with no paved walks at all and be paved only after a season, along the lines its walkers have worn.
V01-C-007: The rectangular street grid is often dismissed as the plan of a surveyor rather than a designer, monotonous and indifferent to the land beneath it. Its defenders reply that this indifference, far from being a weakness, is precisely its strength. Because every block resembles every other, no block is committed in advance to a particular use, and a district laid out for warehouses can later fill with flats or offices. Winding medieval streets, by contrast, were shaped around the markets, walls and landholdings of their own time, and they tend to resist uses their builders never imagined. Seen beside such streets, the grid looks less like a design for one city than a framework within which many cities can succeed one another.
V01-C-008: River deltas are, in a sense, always sinking, as the soft sediment that forms them slowly compacts under its own weight. For most of their history this loss was made good by floods, which spread fresh silt across the land and raised it a little each season. Embankments built to keep those floods out of farms and towns have broken the cycle, so that much of the sediment now runs straight to the sea. Deprived of its yearly supply, the land goes on settling, and in places it now lies lower relative to the river than it did before the embankments were raised. The defences are thus caught in a loop of their own making: the more completely they keep the river out, the further the land behind them falls, and the higher they must be raised.
V01-C-009: When a congested road is widened, traffic usually flows faster for the first few months. The quicker journey, though, tempts people who had been travelling at other hours, by other routes or not at all. Within a few years the new lanes are often as crowded as the old ones were, carrying more cars at much the same speed. Widening a road, then, may do less to relieve congestion than to enlarge the amount of driving the road must carry.
V01-C-010: If you have promised to help a friend move house on Saturday and your child falls ill on Friday night, almost everyone agrees that you should stay at home. One view holds that the promise has simply lapsed, since every promise carries an unspoken condition that nothing serious intervenes. The difficulty with this view is that you still owe your friend something: an apology, an explanation, perhaps an offer to help another day. Such lingering debts suggest that the promise was outweighed rather than cancelled, and an outweighed obligation leaves a trace that a lapsed one would not.
V01-C-011: If every plank of a ship is replaced one by one over many years, most people are content to say that it remains the same ship. Their confidence is shaken when they learn that someone has kept the discarded planks and assembled them, in the original arrangement, into a second vessel. Now two ships have a claim to the original's identity, one by continuity of form and use, the other by continuity of material. That the puzzle arises only when both claims are pressed at once suggests that our idea of sameness serves several purposes, which ordinarily coincide and only occasionally come apart.
V01-C-012: Some legal systems impose no general duty to rescue a stranger, even when rescue would cost the bystander almost nothing. This strikes most people as morally perverse, since a passer-by who watches a child drown in shallow water seems plainly to have done wrong. Defenders of the rule reply that the law must draw lines it can enforce, and that a duty to rescue has no natural limit once the cost of helping is allowed to grow. Their worry, in other words, is not that the bystander is blameless but that a court cannot say how much he should have risked.
V01-C-013: Philosophers often test a theory by imagining an unusual case and asking whether the theory's verdict on it seems right. Critics object that such verdicts are unreliable, since the same case can draw different responses when it is described in different words or put to different audiences. The objection proves less than it seems to, because ordinary perception is open to the same charge, and nobody concludes that we should stop trusting our eyes. What we do instead is learn the conditions under which sight misleads, and correct for them. A careful philosopher can treat intuitions in the same way, as evidence that is fallible in known ways rather than as an oracle or as mere noise.
V01-C-014: A confident eyewitness is among the most persuasive figures in a courtroom, and jurors tend to treat certainty as a sign of accuracy. The trouble is that confidence can grow after the event for reasons that have nothing to do with what was seen. A witness who picks a suspect from a line-up and is then told he chose correctly will often recall being surer than he was, so his later certainty reflects the encouragement as much as the glimpse. For this reason, some researchers argue that only the confidence a witness expresses at the first identification, before any feedback, deserves much weight.
V01-C-015: A student who fails repeatedly at a subject, whatever he does, may stop trying even when success later comes within reach. Teachers sometimes read this withdrawal as laziness, but it is closer to a reasonable conclusion drawn from experience. The conclusion is that effort makes no difference, and for this student, so far, it has been true. The remedy, accordingly, is not exhortation but a run of tasks in which effort visibly pays, so that the conclusion is overturned by fresh evidence rather than by argument.
V01-C-016: Boredom is usually treated as a defect of the situation, the mark of a lecture too slow or a task too repetitive. It may be better understood as a signal, much as pain is, telling us that what we are doing has stopped repaying the attention we give it. Seen this way, the habit of relieving every idle moment with a screen looks less like a cure than like taking painkillers for an injury one never examines. The discomfort is muffled, but the information it carried, that something in one's activity ought to change, goes unread. None of this makes boredom pleasant, or the screen an enemy; it suggests only that the urge to escape may be worth hearing out before it is silenced.
V01-C-017: People often describe their best hours of work as times when they lost track of the clock and forgot themselves in the task. Psychologists who have studied such states find that they arise most readily when a task is hard enough to demand full attention but not so hard as to provoke anxiety. Too easy a task leaves room for the mind to wander, while too difficult a one fills it with worry about failure. Since each of these failures is a failure of fit, the absorption people prize is less a gift of temperament than a product of the match between their skill and the challenge before them.
V01-C-018: A museum label seems the most modest of texts, a few lines giving a name, a date and a material. Yet even this minimum involves a choice about what kind of thing the object is. A mask described only by its wood and its century is being presented as a sculpture to be looked at, rather than as an object that was once worn, danced in and perhaps feared. Adding a paragraph about its ceremonial use does not escape the difficulty, since that too selects one story about the mask from among several. If neither the bare label nor the long one is neutral, the honest course is not to search for neutrality but to let visitors see that a choice has been made.
V01-C-019: Older recipes are often maddeningly vague, calling for a handful of flour, butter the size of an egg, or an oven that is moderately hot. Modern readers tend to see this vagueness as a failure of precision, which later cookbooks corrected with level cups, exact weights and oven temperatures. But the older writers were not failing at precision; they were addressing cooks who had learned by watching and could judge the feel of a dough better than any measure could describe it. Exact quantities became necessary only when such cooks gave way to readers who learned from books, with no one at their elbow to show them.
V01-C-020: It is often said that the decline of the handwritten letter has made our private lives shallower. Anyone who reads through an old family's correspondence, however, will find that most of the letters were dutiful reports of health, weather and the price of things. What has really been lost is not depth of feeling but a durable record, since letters were kept in drawers while much of what replaced them is deleted or never written down. It may be historians, then, rather than the people who once had to write them, who have most reason to miss the letters.
V01-C-021: A familiar objection to free lending libraries is that nobody will buy a book that can be borrowed for nothing. The objection treats readers as a fixed population, each of whom will obtain a given book in one way or another. But readers are made, not found, and a child who grows up near a library is likely to become an adult who buys books as well as borrowing them. This reply does not settle every case, since a popular novel borrowed fifty times may indeed have cost its author several sales. Even so, a trade that depends on a reading public has reason to welcome the institution that does most to create one.
V01-C-022: Salt was once among the most reliable things a government could tax. Everyone needed it, rich and poor alike, and in many regions it could be produced only at a few coastal pans or mines that officials could easily watch. These same features, however, made the tax unusually resented, since it fell hardest on the poor, who spent a larger share of their income on necessities. Salt duties thus became a recurring grievance in popular protest, precisely because they were so efficient at raising money.
V01-C-023: Term limits are usually defended as a check on entrenched power, a way of ensuring that no officeholder grows too comfortable to be removed. The argument assumes that voters, left to themselves, will not reliably remove a leader who has outstayed his usefulness. The assumption is not as insulting as it sounds: voters may be sensible and still face an incumbent with advantages in money, publicity and patronage that no challenger can match. Even so, a limit removes the competent along with the complacent, and it hands the last years of every final term to a leader who no longer needs anyone's approval. Whether the trade is worth making depends less on any principle than on how unequal elections in a given country actually are.
V01-C-024: The roads the Romans built across their empire were laid out chiefly for the rapid movement of soldiers, not for the convenience of traders. Once built, however, they served everyone who could use them, and merchants, officials and letters travelled along them as readily as legions. Towns grew up at their junctions and river crossings, and some of these places are still inhabited where the old routes met. A network designed to hold territory by force thus ended by shaping the economic life of a continent long after the force was gone.
V01-C-025: Political writers have long warned against hiring soldiers, arguing that men who fight for pay will desert the moment a battle turns against them. Yet rulers went on hiring them regardless, and they did so not only out of necessity. An army of armed citizens could turn its weapons on the government that raised it, whereas a hired company had no stake in local quarrels. Its loyalty was narrow but predictable: it served whoever paid, for as long as he paid. The real danger, then, lay less on the battlefield than in the treasury, since a ruler who ran out of money might find his own unpaid soldiers camped outside his gates.
